title: Growing Taller: How Kids' Bodies Grow
summary: How growth plates near the ends of bones build new bone, how growth hormone from a small brain gland drives this, and how sleep, nutrition, and genes all shape how a child grows.
poll: Sleep matters just as much as food for growing taller.

versions.title: Growing Taller
versions.text:
Every year, you grow a bit taller. How does your body do that?

Your body has many bones. Bones hold you up.

Near the end of each bone is a soft spot. It is a growth plate. It is not hard like the rest of the bone.

The growth plate makes new bone. The bone gets longer. That makes you taller.

A small gland is deep in your brain. It makes a hormone. The hormone tells your body to grow.

Your body makes more of it when you sleep. That is why sleep helps you grow.

Food helps too. Milk, eggs, and meat help build new bone.

Genes from your mom and dad play a part. They help set how tall you may grow.

When you are older, growth plates close. The bone turns hard. Then you stop growing taller.

versions.title: Growing Taller

Every year, you grow a bit taller. How does your body make that happen?

Your body has many bones. Bones hold your whole body up.

Near the end of each bone is a soft spot. It is called a growth plate. It is not hard like the rest of the bone.

The growth plate makes new bone, little by little. The bone gets a bit longer. That is part of how you grow taller.

A small gland sits deep inside your brain. It makes a hormone. This hormone tells your body to grow.

Your body makes more of this hormone while you sleep. That is one reason sleep helps you grow.

Food helps too. Milk, eggs, and other healthy foods give your body what it needs to build new bone.

Genes from your mom and dad play a part too. They help set how tall you may grow.

When you get older, your growth plates slowly close. The soft spot turns into hard bone. After that, you stop growing taller.

versions.title: Growing Taller: How Kids' Bodies Grow
versions.text:
Every year, almost without noticing, a growing child becomes a little bit taller. How does the body bring about this gradual, ongoing process?

The human skeleton is made up of many bones, and these bones support the entire body while giving it its overall shape.

Near the end of each long bone lies a soft region called a growth plate, made of a flexible material called cartilage rather than hard bone. This lets the bone keep lengthening throughout childhood.

The growth plate steadily produces new bone, little by little, across many months and years, and each time it does, the bone becomes slightly longer, which is part of how the body grows taller.

A small gland deep inside the brain, called the pituitary gland, releases growth hormone. This hormone travels through the blood and signals bone tissue throughout the body to continue growing.

The pituitary gland releases more growth hormone during deep sleep than during the daytime, which helps explain why sufficient, high-quality sleep is so important for healthy growth.

If the pituitary gland does not make enough of this hormone, doctors call the condition a growth hormone deficiency, and children with this condition can often be treated with extra hormone from a doctor.

Good nutrition matters a great deal as well, since food supplies nutrients, including protein, calcium, and vitamins, that the body requires to build new bone.

Hereditary factors inherited from a child's parents also matter considerably, helping to regulate a general range within which that person is likely to grow.

Sleep, nutrition, and heredity work together to regulate growth, and none of these three factors can fully replace either of the other two. Eventually, during the teenage years, growth plates close through a process called ossification, hardening into solid bone, after which a person stops growing taller.

The human skeleton is composed of many bones, and these bones support the entire body while providing its overall structure and shape.

The growth plate steadily produces new bone tissue, little by little, across many months and years, and each time it does so, the bone becomes slightly longer, which is part of how the body gradually grows taller over time.

A small gland situated deep inside the brain, called the pituitary gland, releases growth hormone. This hormone travels through the bloodstream and signals bone tissue throughout the body to continue growing steadily.

If the pituitary gland fails to produce enough of this hormone, doctors describe the resulting condition as a growth hormone deficiency, and children affected by it can often be treated successfully with supplemental hormone prescribed by a doctor.

Good nutrition matters tremendously as well, since food supplies essential nutrients, including protein, calcium, and various vitamins, that the body requires in order to build new bone tissue.

Hereditary factors inherited from a child's parents also matter considerably, helping to regulate a general range within which that particular individual is likely to grow.

Sleep, nutrition, and heredity work together continuously to regulate growth, and none of these three factors can fully substitute for either of the other two. versions.title: Growing Taller: How Kids' Bodies Grow
versions.text:
Every year, almost without noticing, a growing child becomes somewhat taller, a change that unfolds so gradually it is rarely perceived day to day. How does the body bring about this ongoing process, year after year, without any conscious effort whatsoever?

The human skeleton is composed of numerous bones, and these bones support the entire body while providing its overall structure and shape.

Near the end of each long bone lies a soft region known as a growth plate, composed of a flexible material called cartilage rather than hard, solid bone. This structure allows the bone to continue lengthening throughout childhood and adolescence, until a certain point is eventually reached.

The growth plate steadily produces new bone tissue, little by little, across many months and years, and each time it does so, the bone becomes slightly longer, which is part of how the body gradually grows taller over an extended period.

A small gland situated deep inside the brain, called the pituitary gland, releases growth hormone, a chemical messenger that travels through the bloodstream and signals bone tissue throughout the body to continue growing steadily.

The pituitary gland releases considerably more growth hormone during deep sleep than during the daytime, which helps explain why sufficient, high-quality sleep remains so essential for healthy, sustained growth.

If the pituitary gland fails to produce enough of this hormone, doctors describe the resulting condition as a growth hormone deficiency, and children affected by it can frequently be treated successfully with supplemental hormone prescribed by a qualified doctor.

Good nutrition matters tremendously as well, since food supplies essential nutrients, including protein, calcium, and various vitamins, that the body requires in order to construct new bone tissue.

Hereditary factors inherited from a child's parents also matter considerably, helping to regulate a general range within which that particular individual is likely to grow.

Sleep, nutrition, and heredity work together continuously to regulate growth, and none of these three factors can fully substitute for either of the other two. A child who sleeps well but rarely consumes nutritious meals, for instance, may still fail to grow as well as their genes would otherwise permit, since all three conditions must be satisfied simultaneously.

Eventually, during the teenage years, growth plates close through a biological process called ossification, hardening permanently into solid bone, after which a person stops growing any taller for the remainder of their life.

versions.title: Growing Taller: How Kids' Bodies Grow
versions.text:
Every year, almost without conscious awareness, a growing child becomes somewhat taller, a transformation that unfolds so gradually it is rarely perceived from one day to the next. How does the body bring about this ongoing process, year after year, entirely without deliberate effort?

The human skeleton is composed of numerous bones, and these bones collectively support the entire body while providing its overall structure and shape.

Near the end of each long bone lies a soft region known as a growth plate, composed of a flexible material called cartilage rather than hard, solid bone. This structure permits the bone to continue lengthening throughout childhood and adolescence, until a particular point is eventually reached.

The growth plate steadily produces new bone tissue, incrementally, across many months and years, and each time it does so, the bone becomes marginally longer, which constitutes part of how the body gradually grows taller over an extended period.

A small gland situated deep within the brain, known as the pituitary gland, releases growth hormone, a chemical messenger that travels through the bloodstream and signals bone tissue throughout the body to continue growing steadily.

The pituitary gland releases considerably more growth hormone during deep sleep than during daytime hours, which helps explain why sufficient, high-quality sleep remains so essential for healthy, sustained growth.

Should the pituitary gland fail to produce adequate amounts of this hormone, physicians describe the resulting condition as a growth hormone deficiency, and children affected by it can frequently be treated successfully with supplemental hormone prescribed by a qualified physician.

Good nutrition matters tremendously as well, since food supplies essential nutrients, including protein, calcium, and various vitamins, that the body requires in order to construct new bone tissue.

Hereditary factors inherited from a child's parents also matter considerably, helping to regulate a general range within which that particular individual is likely to grow, since the height of close biological relatives tends to predict, though never precisely determine, a child's own eventual adult height.

Sleep, nutrition, and heredity work together continuously to regulate growth, and none of these three factors can fully substitute for either of the remaining two. A child who sleeps well but rarely consumes nutritious meals, for instance, may still fail to grow as well as their genes would otherwise permit, since all three conditions must be satisfied simultaneously for optimal growth to occur.

Eventually, during the teenage years, growth plates close through a biological process called ossification, hardening permanently into solid bone, after which a person stops growing any taller for the remainder of their life.

Should the pituitary gland fail to produce adequate quantities of this hormone, physicians describe the resulting condition as a growth hormone deficiency, and children affected by it can frequently be treated successfully with supplemental hormone prescribed by a qualified physician.

MID.modelAnswer: A small gland deep in the brain releases growth hormone, which travels through the blood and signals the body to keep growing. The body releases more of this hormone during deep sleep, so getting enough sleep supports healthy growth. At the same time, food supplies nutrients like protein and calcium that the body needs to build new bone, and genes inherited from a child's parents help set a general range for how tall that child may grow.

keyWords.definition: describing a small gland at the base of the brain that releases growth hormone and other hormones
keyWords.example: A doctor can check whether the pituitary gland is releasing enough growth hormone.

keyWords.definition: the process by which soft tissue, such as cartilage, hardens into bone
keyWords.example: Ossification continues throughout childhood, gradually turning cartilage into solid bone.

keyWords.definition: passed down from parents to their children through genes
keyWords.example: Eye color is a hereditary trait passed down within a family.

keyWords.definition: a lack or shortage of something the body needs
keyWords.example: A vitamin deficiency can sometimes be treated with the right supplement.

keyWords.definition: to control or adjust something so it works properly
keyWords.example: A thermostat helps regulate the temperature inside a house.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Height is decided entirely by how much a child eats
Growth hormone deficiency affects every child equally
Hormone, nutrition, and heredity jointly regulate growth
Ossification happens only in children who sleep poorly
questions.why: The article traces how the pituitary gland's growth hormone, nutrition, and hereditary factors together regulate how tall a child grows.

wrong.A: The article presents height as shaped by several factors, not diet alone.
wrong.B: A growth hormone deficiency is described as a specific, treatable condition, not something affecting every child.
wrong.D: Ossification is a normal process linked to age, not specifically to poor sleep.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does the pituitary gland release that signals the body to grow?
options: A mineral called calcium
A chemical called growth hormone
A soft tissue called cartilage
A nutrient called vitamin D
questions.why: The article states the pituitary gland releases growth hormone, which signals bone tissue to continue growing.

wrong.A: Calcium comes from food, not the pituitary gland.
wrong.C: Cartilage makes up the growth plate; it is not released by the gland.
wrong.D: Vitamin D comes from food or sunlight, not the pituitary gland.

questions.stem: Based on the article, when does the pituitary gland release the most growth hormone?
options: During deep sleep at night
During the middle of the afternoon
Right after a large meal
During intense physical exercise
questions.why: The article says the pituitary gland releases considerably more growth hormone during deep sleep than during the daytime.

wrong.B: The article contrasts deep sleep with daytime, which includes the afternoon.
wrong.C: Meals are linked to nutrition, not directly to hormone timing in the article.
wrong.D: Exercise is not mentioned as a trigger for releasing growth hormone.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word hereditary mean?
options: Passed down from parents to children
Added through healthy eating habits
Removed by a doctor's treatment
Created only during deep sleep
questions.why: The article describes hereditary factors as ones inherited from a child's parents.

wrong.B: Nutrition is a separate factor from heredity in the article.
wrong.C: Hereditary factors are inherited, not removed by treatment.
wrong.D: Heredity comes from parents, not from sleep.

questions.stem: How does the article organize its explanation after describing the growth plate?
options: By comparing the heights of children in different countries
By explaining the hormone, then sleep, nutrition, and heredity
By listing the dates of famous height records in the world
By telling a long story about one tall athlete and his team
questions.why: After describing the growth plate, the article explains the pituitary gland's hormone, then moves through sleep, nutrition, and heredity in turn.

wrong.A: The article does not compare children across countries.
wrong.C: No historical height records are listed.
wrong.D: The article is not a personal narrative about an athlete.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is the effect of a growth hormone deficiency?
options: A child's growth plates close much earlier than normal
A child's bones become permanently unbreakable
A child's genes change to a different pattern
A child may not grow as expected without treatment
questions.why: The article says a growth hormone deficiency can be treated with supplemental hormone, implying that without treatment, growth may not proceed as expected.

wrong.A: The article does not link a hormone deficiency to earlier closing of growth plates.
wrong.B: Unbreakable bones are not discussed in the article.
wrong.C: A hormone deficiency does not change a person's genes.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the article's description of sleep, nutrition, and heredity?
options: Any single one of the three factors is enough alone
Heredity matters far more than the other two factors
All three factors must work together for healthy growth
None of the three factors affects height at all
questions.why: The article states that none of the three factors can fully substitute for the other two, meaning all three must work together.

wrong.A: The article explicitly says no single factor can replace the others.
wrong.B: The article gives sleep, nutrition, and heredity comparable importance.
wrong.D: The article closely links all three factors to growth.

questions.stem: A doctor notices a child sleeps well and eats well but has unusually short parents. What would the article most likely say?
options: The child's height may still be influenced by heredity
The child should stop sleeping early to grow taller
The child's growth plates will never close
The child definitely has a growth hormone deficiency
questions.why: The article says hereditary factors inherited from parents help regulate a child's general range of height, which could apply here even with good sleep and nutrition.

wrong.B: The article presents sleep as something that helps growth, not something to reduce.
wrong.C: Growth plates are described as eventually closing for everyone.
wrong.D: A hormone deficiency is a specific condition and cannot be assumed from this information alone.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the pituitary gland, sleep, nutrition, and heredity each regulate how a child grows taller. Use specific evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained the pituitary gland's role in releasing growth hormone.
I described how sleep, nutrition, and heredity each affect growth, using evidence from the article.
I connected ideas with transition words such as therefore, as a result, or because.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The pituitary gland releases growth hormone, which travels through the bloodstream and signals bone tissue to keep growing, and it releases considerably more of this hormone during deep sleep than during the day. As a result, consistent sleep supports healthy growth, while good nutrition supplies nutrients such as protein and calcium that the body needs to build new bone. Hereditary factors inherited from a child's parents also regulate a general range for height, so because none of these three factors can fully replace the others, all of them must work together until growth plates eventually close through ossification.
